newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Impact of latest Brazil financial moves seen small.
newsitem.headline: Impact of latest Brazil financial moves seen small.

text.p: Brazil's latest bid to boost the influx of foreign capital will raise dollar flows only slightly and do little to ease the nation's swelling current account gap, economists said.
"The impression I have is that the direct impact on the balance of payments will be small," said economist Marcelo Audi of Merrill Lynch & Co Inc in Sao Paulo.

The National Monetary Council (CMN) on Wednesday ruled that banks raising funds abroad for loans to local firms under Resolution 63 may invest the money in dollar-indexed National Treasury Notes (NTN-D) if the funds are not immediately loaned out.

This allows the banks to arbitrage on the money -- a turnaround from a restriction imposed a year ago. That rule only allowed banks to deposit the money with the Central Bank, where it would earn the London Inter-Bank Offered Rate (Libor) -- effectively wiping out the possibility of arbitrage.
The CMN, the policy-making arm of the Central Bank, also approved an income tax exemption for the earnings of foreign capital funds that invest in emerging companies.
"The basic idea of these two measures was to increase the amount of foreign capital coming into Brazilian markets," said Marcelo Allain of BMC Bank in Brazil.
By enlarging foreign currency inflow, the Central Bank hopes to boost reserves, enabling it to more easily finance the current account gap and stave off potential problems from its steady widening.

The move to allow banks to invest in NTN-Ds will improve the financial climate in Brazil, encouraging banks to go abroad to raise funds and thereby "ease the process of rolling over bonds and commercial paper issued in the past," said BMC's Allain said.

But economists said the impact on the current account gap will be small and the rise in capital flows limited because local interest rates have fallen sharply since last year. NTN-D rates have fallen to around 11.5 percent from roughly 15.4 percent a year ago.
"The arbitrage rate is much less now than it was when they imposed restrictions a year ago," said economist Marcelo Carvalho of J.P. Morgan's Brazilian unit.
"It will have some impact, but not a dramatic one," he added.
The moves are only the latest steps taken by the government to contain the current account gap, which has widened primarily by Brazil's growing trade deficit.
In May, the Central Bank discouraged credit card use abroad and lifted a 1995 ban on foreign participation in the derivatives market to hedge financial transactions.
Two months earlier, the bank adopted measures to control the trade deficit and protect Brazil's $58 billion in reserves. Reserves have slipped from a high of $59.23 billion in November 1996.
By year's end, economists expect the current account gap to reach between four and five percent of gross domestic product and the trade deficit to rise to $12 billion.
The current account gap now stands at about four percent while the trade deficit is already above $4.0 billion.
